title: Read the label, not the rumour
task: Match each thing on the record to what it lets you conclude.
scene: A fire at the freight yard has damaged several unlabelled drums, eighty metres from the river. Three different guesses are already on the radio. Firefighters are choosing what to spray based on whatever you tell them.
takeaway: A name is a label. A formula says what something is made of, which is what decides how it behaves.
why: A formula says which elements are in something and how many of each. That is what decides how it behaves: what it dissolves in, what it reacts with, what it does to water.
answerText: 1. The formula pairs a metal with a charged group of atoms. → Likely an ionic compound. 2. Two substances share the same elements but different ratios. → They are distinct compounds, not interchangeable names. 3. A particle has more electrons than protons. → It is negatively charged. 4. A label gives a common name with no composition or concentration. → The record is insufficient for hazard prediction.

choices: Probably one of the salts — held together by opposite charges.
Not one material under two labels — these behave differently.
It carries a negative charge overall.
Not enough to say anything about the danger.
rebuttals: A metal with a charged group of atoms is the usual sign of a salt. Two opposite charges holding on to each other.
Change how many of each and you change what it does. The counts are part of the identity.
More electrons than protons means extra negative charge. Counting the two is the whole test.
A trade name with no formula and no strength says nothing about danger. It is a word on a drum.
scenarios: A metal, paired with a charged group of atoms.
Two records share every element and disagree on how many of each.
A particle has more electrons than protons.
A label gives a trade name and nothing else.
text.setup: Match each formula-level observation to the correct chemical interpretation.
text.call: Read the formula, not the rumor

title: From damaged drum to a first answer
task: Put the four steps in order of what each one costs, cheapest first.
scene: In the mobile laboratory, the first sealed drum sample is on the bench. The markings on the outside are readable now, and opening the drum will scuff them off. Opening it also lets the air above the liquid escape. There is enough liquid for two tests.
takeaway: Do the tests that cost nothing before the ones that cannot be taken back.
why: The order is set by what each step costs. The markings on the outside survive only until somebody opens the drum. So they get photographed first, and that costs nothing. Sampling the air above the liquid takes what has already escaped. Nothing has to be opened for it.
answerText: 1. Photograph and record the markings on the outside of the drum, which consumes nothing. 2. Sample the headspace vapour onto a sorbent tube, without breaching the bulk liquid. 3. Draw a small aliquot and run a non-destructive spectrum on it. 4. Commit part of that aliquot to a method that destroys it to identify it.

rebuttals: Photograph first. It costs nothing, and it is the only evidence that stops existing the moment the drum is opened.
The air above the liquid second. It samples what has already got out, without breaching anything.
A test that gives the sample back third. A mistake there costs nothing at all.
The test that uses it up last. It answers best and it answers once, so spend it when you know what to ask.
cards: Photograph the markings on the outside, which uses nothing up.
Collect the air above the liquid, without opening the drum.
Take a few drops, and run a test that gives them back.
Run the test that uses up the sample.
text.setup: Order the non-destructive evidence workflow.
text.call: From damaged container to provisional identity

title: Float or sink
task: Spend the budget on the evidence that could change the answer.
scene: One drum is leaking into the bund. Nobody knows what the liquid is yet. Adaeze Okonjo needs to know whether it will float on the water already lying there, or sink under it.
question: Which measurement decides whether the liquid floats on water?
takeaway: Whether something floats is a comparison, not a property: it is heavier or lighter than the same amount of water.
why: Floating is a comparison. A litre of water weighs about a kilogram, so a litre of anything lighter than that rides on top and a litre of anything heavier goes under. Nothing else on the list decides it. Colour and smell say nothing about weight.
answerText: How much a litre of it weighs. Under a kilogram and it floats, over a kilogram and it sinks.

choices: How much a litre of it weighs
What colour it is
How strongly it smells
How much of it is in the drum
rebuttals: Colour is worth writing down and decides nothing here. Clear liquids do both.
Smell is a warning, not a measurement, and it means putting somebody in the vapour.
A spoonful and a full drum of the same liquid float exactly alike.
text.setup: One drum is leaking into the bund, and nobody knows what the liquid is.

title: The wind changes the map
task: Choose who gets the warning first.
scene: Erik Lindqvist, the dispersion modeller, pins a wind arrow over the city map. A gas cloud is moving away from the freight yard. The school and two neighborhoods sit in different directions.
question: The wind arrow points toward the school. What should happen first?
takeaway: Gases spread out, but wind decides which direction gets the danger first.
why: The cloud does not threaten every place equally at the same moment. Wind carries it downwind. The safest first move is to warn and move the people in its path while teams keep checking the wind.
answerText: Warn and move the school first, then keep updating the plan if the wind changes.

choices: Warn the school and start moving students now.
Wait until the exact chemical is known.
Evacuate the neighborhood upwind first.
Close the river path and do nothing else yet.
rebuttals: Identity matters, but the wind has already told you who is in the path.
Upwind is where the cloud is moving away from.
Closing one path does not protect the people directly downwind.
text.answer: Warn the school and start moving students now.

title: What changes the cloud
task: Match each change in the field to what it does.
scene: The weather station shows the temperature rising and the pressure falling, with the wind picking up. Crews report vapour pooling in a low channel downwind.
takeaway: Some things change what the gas is doing. Others change where it is going. They are not the same question.
why: Two different things are happening at once. Warming a gas makes it take up more room, and dropping the pressure around it does the same. That is about the gas itself.
answerText: 1. Temperature rises at roughly constant pressure. → Volume rises in proportion to the absolute temperature. 2. External pressure falls for the same gas amount and temperature. → Volume rises in inverse proportion to the pressure. 3. A gas has greater molar mass than surrounding air. → It may initially favour lower-level accumulation, though turbulence matters. 4. Wind direction shifts while the source continues. → The downwind risk corridor must be updated.

choices: It takes up more room, in step with the warming.
It takes up more room, with less pushing in.
It may sink and pool low down.
The danger has moved, so the map must move.
rebuttals: Warming a gas at the same pressure makes it swell, in step with the warming.
Less pressure pushing in on the same gas lets it swell out. Half the pressure, twice the room.
Being heavier than air decides whether it sinks or lifts, and stirring by the wind can beat it.
A wind shift moves where it goes and changes nothing about the gas itself.
scenarios: The temperature rises, with the pressure much the same.
The pressure falls, with the same gas and the same warmth.
The gas is heavier than air.
The wind shifts while the drum is still leaking.
text.setup: Match each change to its first-order consequence.

title: Why the drum is worse in the afternoon
task: Say why the same drum reads three times higher.
scene: The same open drum reads three times the vapour at two in the afternoon as it did at six in the morning. Nothing has been added and nothing taken out.
question: Same drum, same liquid, three times the vapour. Why?
takeaway: A measurement of a hazard belongs to the conditions it was taken in.
why: A liquid is always losing molecules into the air above it, and getting some back. How many are up there at once depends on temperature, and it climbs steeply. Ten or fifteen degrees can double it.
answerText: It warmed up. A warmer liquid puts far more of itself into the air above it, with nothing else changing at all.

choices: Warmer liquid puts more of itself into the air.
It reacted during the day and made something that evaporates faster.
The morning reading was wrong, because instruments drift when cold.
More evaporated overnight, so what is left is stronger.
rebuttals: Something new would show up as a different substance, and the analysis shows the same one.
Both readings came from the same instrument, and three times over is far more than it can drift.
Evaporating takes away the part that evaporates most easily, which would lower the vapour rather than raise it.

title: Where will it go?
task: Match each kind of chemical to where it ends up.
scene: Runoff from the fire has reached the river. Predict the wrong place and the team samples the wrong thing, and a clean water result gets read by the city as an all-clear.
takeaway: Not finding something in the water does not mean it is not in the river.
why: Where a chemical goes follows from what it is like. Some dissolve straight into water and travel with it. Some refuse to mix at all, and sit on top as a film or sink underneath as a layer.
answerText: 1. Small ionic species in water. → Often dissolves as hydrated ions. 2. Nonpolar organic liquid that barely mixes with water. → May form a separate phase or surface film. 3. Polar neutral molecule capable of hydrogen bonding. → Often has appreciable water solubility. 4. Water-avoiding compound that sticks strongly to organic-rich sediment. → May concentrate in suspended particles or sediment.

choices: Spread right through the water, travelling with it.
Sits as a separate layer or a film on the surface.
Dissolves well, and moves with the water.
Rides the specks down, and ends up in the mud.
rebuttals: Something that dissolves easily spreads through the water and goes wherever the water goes.
An oily liquid barely mixes at all. It makes its own layer, often a film on top.
Something that mixes the way sugar does dissolves well and travels with the water.
Something that sticks to dirt leaves the water with the dirt, and the dirt settles on the bottom.
scenarios: Something that dissolves easily in water.
An oily liquid that will not mix with water.
Something that mixes with water the way sugar does.
Something that sticks hard to specks of dirt in the water.
columns: What kind of chemical it is
text.setup: Match each molecular feature to the most likely environmental behavior.

title: Pick the right way to separate it
task: Match each mixture to the separation trick that can actually work.
scene: Inês Ferreira, the water and sediment lead, sets four jars on the bench. Some material is floating, some has settled, some is dissolved, and some is mixed as droplets. You have four tools and one try for each jar.
question: Which separation method fits each kind of mixture?
takeaway: You separate a mixture by using a difference between its parts.
why: Different mixtures need different tricks. A filter can catch solid pieces but not something dissolved. Settling works when one part sinks. A floating layer can be skimmed. A dissolved material may need a treatment that turns it into something a filter can catch.
answerText: Use settling for sinking solids, skimming for a floating layer, filtering for solid particles, and treatment-then-filtering for material that is truly dissolved.

choices: Let it settle
Skim the top layer
Run it through a filter
Treat it so a solid forms, then filter
rebuttals: Settling works when gravity can pull solid pieces down.
Skimming works when one liquid floats as a separate layer.
A filter catches particles that are already solid.
Dissolved material can pass through a filter until a treatment changes its form.

scenarios.label: Metal dissolved so the water looks clear

title: Spend the river survey
task: Spend the twenty bottles so the survey can answer all three questions.
scene: The survey has twenty bottles. The chemical barely dissolves, the river runs nine hundred metres from the spill to the water intake, and two samples taken so far disagree six times over.
question: How do you spend twenty bottles without leaving a question unanswered?
takeaway: A sampling plan is the set of questions it can answer, and every bottle spent is a question given up.
why: Three questions need answering and each needs its own bottles. What is reaching the intake now, which is what the city acts on today. What the river looked like before the spill, which is the only way to know whether a reading is unusual.
answerText: Spend most of them on the intake over time, on upstream water, and on the mud and the specks in the water. The stained bank is what to give up.

text.setup: The utility wants an answer this week. What does the survey sample?

allocate.hint: Select sampling packages until the required decision questions are all answerable. The panel updates which questions your current bottle allocation can support.

items.label: Detailed sampling of the visibly stained bank

shape.hint: Select sampling packages until the required decision questions are all answerable. The panel updates which questions your current bottle allocation can support.

title: Undo the dilution
task: Work out what was really in the river sample.
scene: The lab watered the sample down before measuring it. So the number is what was in the vial, not the river. It is in mg/L, which means milligrams in every litre. The city is about to hold that number against a limit.
question: What was really in the river sample?
takeaway: What was done to a sample before it was measured is part of the answer.
why: Samples get watered down so the reading lands inside the range the instrument can measure. That has to be undone before the number means anything about the river. Ten millilitres made up to a hundred is ten times weaker, so the river figure is ten times the reading.
answerText: Twenty-five milligrams a litre. The reading was 2.5, and the sample had been watered down ten times.

text.setup: A river sample is diluted before analysis.

estimate.prompt: Ten millilitres of river water were made up to a hundred millilitres. The instrument then read 2.5 milligrams a litre.
estimate.question: What was really in the river sample?
estimate.relationship: River figure = the reading × the final volume ÷ the sample taken.
estimate.explanation: Ten times weaker means the answer is ten times the reading. Report the reading as it stands and the river looks ten times cleaner than it is.
labels: 2.5 mg/L — milligrams in every litre (what the instrument read)
100 mL (what it was made up to)
10 mL (how much river water was used)

title: Say what should happen, then check
task: Predict what watering it down does, do it, and check the reading.
scene: The reading is above the range this meter was calibrated for. Calibration is the check against known samples. It is what turns a signal into a number. The meter still prints one, and it is going into a report.
question: What should the reading become after watering it down, and does the rerun agree?
takeaway: Predict what a change should do, make it, and check. That is what turns a reading into a result.
why: Above the range it was set up for, an instrument still prints a number, and nobody knows what it means. Watering the sample down by half should halve the reading, and that is a prediction worth making before doing it. A reading of 1.34 should become about 0.67.
answerText: Predict about 0.67, water it down by half, and rerun. The 0.68 that comes back agrees, so doubling it back gives an answer worth reporting.

text.setup: Match each problem to the correction.

verify.decision: Can this sample be reported from an in-range measurement rather than an extrapolation?
verify.hint: Lock the absorbance you expect after a 1:1 dilution. Make the dilution, then spend the verification run; a successful dilution is not evidence until the rerun is measured.

measurements.label: Rerun it diluted, inside the range the instrument was checked against

shape.decision: Can this sample be reported from an in-range measurement rather than an extrapolation?
shape.hint: Lock the absorbance you expect after a 1:1 dilution. Make the dilution, then spend the verification run; a successful dilution is not evidence until the rerun is measured.

title: Map the river with thirty samples
task: Make the city-safety call before the next field report lands.
scene: The city wants a picture of eleven kilometres of river. The laboratory can run thirty samples. The field kit is far rougher than the laboratory.
question: You cannot sample every metre. Where do the samples go?
takeaway: Good numbers in the wrong places and rough numbers in the right ones both mislead.
why: There are two ways to waste this. Perfect chemistry at points nobody cares about, or lots of samples with a kit whose numbers nobody trusts. Both give a confident map that misleads. Every decision the city makes happens at the water intake, so that is where the detail belongs.
answerText: Thickly round the drinking water intake. That is where every decision gets made, and detail anywhere else is detail nobody acts on.

choices: Thickly, round the drinking water intake.
Spread along the river, above and below, over several days.
Into repeats and checks at the places already planned.
Wherever the water looks stained.
rebuttals: Spreading along the river shows where it is going, and it is the second question rather than the first.
Repeats and checks make each number trustworthy and place none of them. That is how you sample, not where.
Sampling the stained water samples the staining. This chemical has no colour at all.
text.setup: You cannot sample every metre of river. Where do the samples go?

title: Where is the heat coming from?
task: Match each temperature clue to what it means.
scene: The fire is out, but one tank is getting warmer. Tomas Brandt, the reactions and energy lead, puts four clues on the board. You have to decide whether heat is leaving, arriving, or still being made.
takeaway: Temperature tells you which way heat is moving. A rising temperature after the fire is out can mean a reaction is still making heat.
why: Heat moves from warmer places to cooler ones. A hot object that is only cooling should get cooler with time. If a tank gets hotter after the fire is out, something is still adding heat and the team must find the source.
answerText: A temperature that keeps rising after the outside fire is gone is the danger clue.

text.setup: Match each clue to the safest interpretation.
choices: Heat is leaving normally.
Heat is still being added.
A large object can hold lots of heat.
Check the sensor before acting on one odd reading.
rebuttals: Cooling means stored heat is moving out.
A continued rise means energy is still arriving from somewhere.
A big warm tank can store much more heat than a small warm cup.
One strange reading should be checked against another sensor.
scenarios: A tank falls from 50°C to 45°C after the fire is out.
A tank rises from 40°C to 47°C after the fire is out.
A huge water bath and a mug both warm by 5°C.
One thermometer jumps while three nearby ones stay steady.

title: Left-over heat, or something still going?
task: Say which explanation fits both bays.
scene: Two bays saw the same fire. Ninety minutes after the cooling stopped, the east bay is cooling and the west bay is warming. The west bay is giving off more gas, and the hot spot has not moved.
question: Is this heat left over, or something still running?
takeaway: A thing that keeps changing after its cause is removed has a cause of its own.
why: Left-over heat can only drain away once the fire is out. That is what the east bay is doing, and it is the control. The west bay is doing the opposite: rising, with more gas coming off, and the hot spot sitting in one place at the drum stack.
answerText: Something is still running in the west bay. Left-over heat drains away, which is what the east bay is doing.

choices: Something is still reacting in the west bay, and making heat.
Heat left over from the fire is still draining away.
The temperature sensors are wrong.
Warm liquid is circulating and carrying heat over there.
Nothing odd. Two bays never cool at the same rate.
choiceMechanisms: It gets hotter after the fire is out, more gas comes off, and the hot spot stays put. That is heat being made.
Something heavy takes hours to give back the heat it soaked up.
All four sensors share one reference, so one bad reference would spoil them all.
Moving liquid carries a hot patch about, and one sensor can catch it.
Two bays that saw the same fire will cool at different speeds.
rebuttals: Left-over heat is exactly what the east bay is doing, which is why the east bay is the control. It cannot rise after the fire goes out.
One shared reference is a real worry and it would move both bays the same way. West rises while east falls.
Moving liquid carries a hot patch around. This hot spot has not moved at all.
Two bays cooling at different speeds is ordinary. One heating while the other cools is not.
text.headline: Ninety minutes after the cooling stopped, the west bay is still climbing.
text.setup: Match each trend to the next interpretation or test.

title: Stop the tank before it runs away
task: Set the warning and stop rules before the temperature trace plays.
scene: The damaged tank is slowly getting hotter even though the fire is out. Tomas Brandt, the reactions and energy lead, says heat can speed some reactions, which can make even more heat. Set the safety rules before the next readings arrive.
takeaway: If a reaction makes heat and heat speeds the reaction, a small rise can feed a dangerous loop.
why: Some reactions happen faster when they are warmer. If that reaction also makes heat, the warming can feed itself. The safe move is to set action points before watching the trace, not after the number has already climbed.
answerText: Set an early warning and a stop/cooling action before the replay starts.

text.setup: Choose the two actions before the temperature trace begins.

trigger.hint: Set each action against the temperature scale, then release the board. The readings arrive afterwards and your own rules decide what happens.

conditions.label: Start extra cooling and alert the team
conditions.action: open the cooling loop and call the team in

conditions.label: Stop feed and isolate the tank
conditions.action: shut the feed line and isolate the tank

shape.hint: Act before the trace reaches the danger zone.

title: Move the water toward neutral
task: Match each pH card to what it means for the plant.
scene: Marisol Reyes, the water utility director, has four pH cards from the intake and treatment tanks. This is the first time you have seen the pH scale.
takeaway: pH tells whether water is acidic, neutral, or basic. Seven is near the middle, and lower numbers are more acidic.
why: For this mission, you only need the direction of the scale. A reading near 7 is the target. Numbers below 7 are acidic; numbers above 7 are basic. Treatment should move the water toward the safe middle without shooting past it.
answerText: Move the treatment reading toward 7, and stop before it swings too far to the other side.

text.setup: Drag each pH card to the correct label.
choices: Neutral or near-neutral
Acidic
More acidic
Basic
rebuttals: Seven is the middle reference used in this mission.
A value below seven is on the acidic side.
Four is farther below seven than six, so it is more acidic.
A value above seven is on the basic side.
scenarios: pH 7
pH 6
pH 4
pH 9

title: Why the first dose overshot
task: Say what the test explains about the overshoot.
scene: A dose worked out from the intake reading overshot badly. The bench test is up beside a curve for a simple acid. That test is a titration: add a little at a time, until the water changes, and count how much it took.
question: Which explanation accounts for the flat stretch and the dose it really took?
takeaway: A reading tells you what is loose right now. It does not tell you what is held in reserve.
why: The reading measures the acid that is loose in the water at that moment. Some acids hold most of theirs back, and release more every time you neutralise what is loose. So the reading looks mild while the amount actually needed is five times bigger.
answerText: The water holds a reserve of acid that the reading cannot see. It lets more out as you neutralise, which is why the dose was five times bigger.

choices: The water holds a reserve of acid that the reading cannot see.
It is a simple acid, and the reading is what it says.
The meter is out of adjustment.
The stuff being added is stronger than the label says.
Nothing odd. Treatment always needs extra.
choiceMechanisms: A long flat stretch and a dose five times bigger is what a hidden reserve does.
Read it, work out the acid, and add the matching amount.
A drifting meter would explain why the sum came out wrong.
Something stronger than labelled would overshoot whatever the water was like.
Operators routinely add extra to be sure.
rebuttals: A simple acid is the reference curve, on the same axes. It finishes early and sharply, and this one does neither.
The meter was checked against two known liquids and it was right. It is answering a different question from the one the dose needed.
Something over-strength would overshoot and it would also finish sooner. This took five times more, not less.
Adding extra is a habit, not an explanation. It cannot produce a flat stretch or a five-fold demand.
text.headline: The intake reads mildly acidic. A dose worked out from that reading overshoots badly.
text.setup: Match each feature to its meaning.

title: Neutralise without overshooting
task: Set the slow-down and stop rules before the stream runs.
scene: The pump is primed and the operators are waiting on the valve. The water is acidic and the iron pipe is corroding. Every change to the pump shows up one reading later.
question: Where do the two thresholds go, when every change shows up a reading late?
takeaway: When the answer arrives late, the rule has to fire early.
why: The pump acts now and the meter shows it later. So waiting until the meter reads what you want guarantees going past it, because more base is already on its way through the tank. Writing the rules first is what stops that.
answerText: Slow the feed near 5.8 and stop it near 6.5. Each change shows up a reading later, so waiting for the number you want arrives too late.

text.setup: The plant wants a neutralisation dose this morning. What do you give them?

trigger.hint: Set both rules before releasing the stream. Each pump command affects the mixed-tank reading one update later, so a threshold set at the final desired reading acts late.

shape.hint: Set both rules before releasing the stream. Each pump command affects the mixed-tank reading one update later, so a threshold set at the final desired reading acts late.

title: Where the metal is going
task: Match each thing happening at the metal to its part in the circuit.
scene: Acidic water is flowing through a section where two different metals are bolted together. An inspection has found one small break in the coating. The team wants the circuit understood before choosing a repair.
takeaway: Rusting is a loop. Break any part of the loop and it stops.
why: Rusting is not simply metal going bad. It is a circuit with four parts: a place losing metal, a place taking the electrons, a path through the metal, and a path through the water. Two different metals bolted together in water provide all four at once.
answerText: 1. Metal atoms lose electrons and enter solution. → Anodic oxidation site. 2. A surface consumes electrons in a reduction reaction. → Cathodic reduction site. 3. Two different metals are electrically connected in an electrolyte. → A galvanic cell can form. 4. A protective coating is breached at one small point. → Localized attack may concentrate at the defect.

choices: This is where the metal is actually being lost.
The other half of the loop, which loses no metal.
Everything the loop needs, in one place.
The whole attack, squeezed into one small spot.
rebuttals: Metal dissolving away is where the loss happens. That is the end of the loop that eats the pipe.
A surface taking the electrons is the other half. It completes the loop and loses nothing itself.
Two different metals in water give a place to lose metal, a place to take electrons, and both paths at once.
One hole in a coating forces the whole attack through one small area, which is why it goes through fast.
scenarios: Metal is dissolving away into the water.
A surface is taking in the electrons that were left behind.
Two different metals are bolted together, in water.
A coating has one small break in it.
columns: What is happening at the metal
Which part of the loop that is
text.setup: Match each observation to the electrochemical role.

title: Which pipe gets the crew first?
task: Use the inspection cards to choose the pipe that needs action now.
scene: Petra Novák, the pipeline maintenance chief, lays out three inspection cards. One pipe is thick and changing slowly. One is thinner but steady. One has only a few millimetres left and is losing metal faster than before.
question: Which pipe should the repair crew isolate first?
takeaway: A damage rate matters most when you compare it with how much material is left.
why: A rate by itself does not tell you whether something is safe. A thin wall that is getting thinner quickly is a more urgent problem than a thick wall changing slowly. The useful question is how fast the safety margin is disappearing.
answerText: Isolate the pipe with only a few millimetres left and a speeding-up loss rate.

choices: The thick pipe losing metal very slowly
The medium pipe with a steady old stain
The thin pipe whose loss rate has sped up
Whichever pipe is closest to the door
rebuttals: It still has a large margin and the loss is slow.
A stain is evidence to inspect, but a steady old mark is less urgent than rapid thinning.
This pipe has the smallest margin and the fastest worsening trend.
Walking distance is not the safety question.
text.answer: The thin pipe whose loss rate has sped up

title: Protect the pipe
task: Say which control goes in first.
scene: The thinnest part of the intake pipe has three millimetres of wall left, and the loss has sped up eight times. The gallery stays cleared until the first control is chosen. Water is still flowing.
question: Which fix breaks the problem most directly?
takeaway: Break the loop where you can break it today, and do the rest afterwards.
why: The loop needs four parts, and breaking any one stops it. The water is acidic, which makes one path easy. The two metals bolted together supply the other. Separating those metals cuts the loop, and it can be done today.
answerText: Separate the two metals where they are bolted together. That breaks the loop directly, and everything else can follow.

choices: Separate the two metals where they are bolted together.
Change the water so it is less aggressive.
Recoat the pipe, and inspect the coating for holes.
Reissue the leak report with the photographs attached.
rebuttals: Changing the water works, and it is tangled up with everything else the treatment has to do, including the neutralising that started this.
A coating blocks one path, and it sends the whole attack through any hole it later gets. That needs inspections with it.
A better-looking report changes nothing in the loop, and it is the intake that is at risk.
text.setup: The corrosion cell is running. Which control goes in first?

dayTitle: Remove It Without Making It Worse
title: What did the treatment actually do?
task: Close the ledger, and find what the water figure does not account for.
scene: The pilot treated a batch holding a hundred kilograms of the chemical. The treated water, the sludge and the gas coming off have each been measured. The city is waiting to hear whether it was destroyed.
question: How much is missing from the measured streams, and does that support destroying it?
takeaway: Taking something out of one place is not destroying it. The ledger has to close.
why: A hundred kilograms went in, and six are left in the water. That is not ninety-four destroyed. Seventy-one are in the sludge and three went off as gas, which is eighty accounted for. Twenty are missing, and the bench has already seen something new that nobody has measured.
answerText: Eighty kilograms are accounted for, so twenty are missing. Until somebody finds those, this is moving it about rather than destroying it.

text.headline: Treated water is down to 6 kg of the 100 kg that went in. The plant is being described as 94% effective.
text.setup: Match each observation to the process implication.
text.call: What did the treatment actually do?

balance.hint: Read every stream first. Count only masses that refer to the same contaminant ledger, then close the difference between the measured outputs and the 100 kg input.

streams.label: Unquantified transformation-product pool
streams.note: A separate analytical signal exists, but the method has not yet converted it to a concentration.

shape.hint: Read every stream first. Count only masses that refer to the same contaminant ledger, then close the difference between the measured outputs and the 100 kg input.

dayTitle: Remove It Without Making It Worse
title: Put the treatment in order
task: Put the four stages in the order they have to run.
scene: Four stages are on the table and the plant wants an order for them. Riverton has one intake, and it cannot run this experiment twice while the water is off.
takeaway: Each stage is ordered by what it leaves the next one to work with.
why: Each stage hands something to the next. The first changes the metal into a form that can turn solid, because nothing later can make a solid out of something that will not make one. Changing the water then actually turns it solid.
answerText: 1. Oxidise the dissolved metal to the oxidation state that forms an insoluble hydroxide. 2. Raise the pH to the window where that hydroxide is least soluble. 3. Settle and filter, taking the solid out of the water. 4. Polish the filtered water on activated carbon for what stayed dissolved.

rebuttals: Changing the form first. Nothing later can make a solid out of something that will not make one.
Changing the water second. This is the step that actually produces the solid.
Settling and filtering third, once there is a solid to catch. Filtering dissolved metal catches nothing.
Carbon last. Send solids into a carbon bed and it clogs within hours, and everything after it stops.
cards: Change the dissolved metal into the form that can turn solid.
Change the water, so that form actually turns solid.
Let it settle, and filter the solid out.
Polish what is left on carbon, for whatever stayed dissolved.
text.setup: Order the decision workflow.

dayTitle: Remove It Without Making It Worse
title: Choose what the pilot measures
task: Make the city-safety call before the next field report lands.
scene: The pilot has room for one question, four weeks, and a tenth of the flow. All three methods claim to remove the chemical, and the full plant is committed in June whatever the pilot finds.
question: All three remove it. What does the pilot have to measure?
takeaway: Measure the thing that would tell the options apart, not the thing they all agree on.
why: Every method here removes the chemical. That is why they are all on the table, and it is why measuring removal cannot choose between them. What separates them is what they leave behind: what the chemical turns into, and where the waste ends up.
answerText: What the chemical turns into. Every method removes it, so removal cannot tell them apart, and what they leave behind can.

choices: What the chemical turns into, and how harmful those things are.
How much of the chemical each method removes, in real river water.
Whether the material wears out, and where the used waste goes.
The highest removal anybody can reach, at any dose.
rebuttals: Comparing removal is the comparison, and judged on that alone it picks whichever method makes the most byproduct fastest.
Whether it wears out and where the waste goes both matter, and they come once a method is chosen. They describe the life of a decision already made.
Chasing the highest removal at any dose is exactly the narrow aim that produced a sludge with twenty kilograms missing from it.
text.setup: All three methods claim removal. What does the pilot have to measure?

title: Two candidates, one difference
task: Say what settles which of the two it is.
scene: Two substances fit the result equally well. Their formulas differ by one oxygen atom. An instrument that weighs molecules has already measured this sample.
question: Two candidates, differing by one oxygen. What settles it?
takeaway: When two answers fit, use a measurement that depends on something they differ in.
why: The two fit the first test equally well. So that test cannot choose between them. What they differ in is weight. One oxygen atom is sixteen units. There is an instrument here that weighs molecules directly. Sixteen units is a huge difference to it.
answerText: Weigh them. One oxygen is sixteen units, which is far more than the instrument that weighs molecules can miss.

choices: The weight of the molecule, which differs by sixteen between them.
The order it came out in, heavier ones later.
How big the peak is, since the heavier one gives more signal.
Neither, because they are the same kind of substance.
rebuttals: What comes out first follows chemistry rather than weight. Heavier things sometimes come out earlier.
How big a peak is depends on how much there is, and on the substance. It says nothing about which one.
Sixteen units apart is easy for an instrument that weighs molecules. That is exactly the tie it is built to break.

title: Close the gaps before release
task: Match each weakness in the evidence to what would close it.
scene: A number can be perfectly correct and still answer the wrong question. The pipes are about to be brought back up to pressure on the strength of this evidence.
takeaway: A correct number is only useful if the sample it came from matches the decision.
why: Each of these is a different kind of gap and none of the fixes swaps for another. Sampling only where the water leaves the plant misses the taps people drink from. Sampling after running the tap for ages measures water nobody receives.
answerText: 1. Only the water leaving the treatment plant was sampled. → Sample representative endpoints and vulnerable zones. 2. Samples from the pipe network were collected after long flushing. → Document flushing and sample under realistic use conditions. 3. The method detection limit exceeds the release limit. → Use a more sensitive validated method. 4. The same laboratory tuned the treatment and then checked the final results. → Add an independent check or review.

choices: Sample at the taps people actually drink from.
Write down the running, and sample the way people really use it.
Get a machine sensitive enough to test the standard.
Get somebody independent to check it.
rebuttals: Sampling where the water leaves the plant misses the taps where people drink. Sample where the exposure happens.
Water sampled after a long run is water nobody receives. Record the running, and sample realistically.
A machine that bottoms out above the legal line cannot test it. That takes a more sensitive one.
One laboratory doing both jobs has marked its own homework. That gap closes with an independent check.
scenarios: Only the water leaving the plant was sampled.
Samples were taken after running the tap for a long time.
Nothing the machine reports can fall under the legal line.
One laboratory both fixed the water and checked it.
text.setup: Match each weakness to the needed evidence.

title: Open, hold, or open with conditions
task: Move and narrow the band, and say whether the valves can open.
scene: The pumps are idle while the board meets. The result is nine against a limit of ten, give or take two. Operators are waiting at the valves, and the city has already been given two different reopening times.
question: Can the whole band be brought under the limit, or only its middle?
takeaway: Moving the middle and narrowing the band are different moves, and a boundary needs both.
why: Nine against a limit of ten looks like a pass until the band is drawn. Give or take two means the honest range runs up to eleven, and eleven is over. A rerun can move the middle without proving the band was too wide.
answerText: Neither move is enough alone. Do both, and the band becomes 8.6 give or take one, with its top edge at 9.6.

text.setup: The verification result is 9 units against a limit of 10, plus or minus 2. What does the board decide?

cloud.hint: Apply the available follow-up evidence and watch both the centre and the width. The release criterion is cleared only when the entire displayed band lies below the boundary.

shape.hint: Apply the available follow-up evidence and watch both the centre and the width. The release criterion is cleared only when the entire displayed band lies below the boundary.

title: What each claim has earned
task: Match each state of the evidence to what should be done with it.
scene: The city wants one sentence, and the chemistry does not support one. Turning all of it into a single green light is how a place gets reopened above a problem nobody wrote down.
takeaway: Readiness is claim by claim. There is no single green light.
why: At the end of this, the evidence sits in four states, and each needs a different sentence. Something confirmed two separate ways can be written down as settled. Something likely, with no way to measure it yet, is provisional, and saying so keeps the record honest.
answerText: 1. Identity confirmed by independent methods and controls. → Treat identity as established with documented methods. 2. A transformation product is plausible but lacks a validated standard. → Label provisional and continue method development. 3. Filtered water meets criteria, but sediment remains contaminated. → Keep managing the sediment, and keep watching for the metal coming back. 4. Pipeline corrosion is controlled only while chemistry remains within a narrow range. → Use conditional operation with chemistry and corrosion triggers.

choices: Write it down as settled, with the methods.
Call it provisional, and keep working on how to measure it.
Keep managing the mud, and keep watching for it coming back.
Keep going under conditions, with triggers written down.
rebuttals: Confirmed two ways with checks is the strongest claim here. Write down the methods and treat it as settled.
Something likely with no way to measure it cannot be quantified yet. Say so, and keep developing the method.
Clean water over dirty mud is a managed situation rather than a solved one, and the managing is what has to continue.
Corrosion held inside a narrow window is conditional. The condition needs triggers, or it is just a hope.
scenarios: Confirmed by two separate methods, with checks.
Likely, and there is no way to measure it yet.
The water passes, and the mud is still contaminated.
Corrosion is under control while the water chemistry holds.
text.setup: Match each evidence state to the correct recommendation.

title: How much did the treatment manage?
task: Compare what the treatment removed with the most it could have removed.
scene: Kwabena Osei has two numbers on the board. The cell could remove at most 4.5 kilograms of metal. The water test says it removed 3.6.
question: What share of the best-case removal did the cell manage?
takeaway: A treatment result is easier to judge when you compare what happened with a clear maximum.
why: Compare what was actually removed against the best case. Three point six out of four point five is four fifths. That is 80 per cent. The electrical details behind the best case are somebody else’s work here. Your job is to judge the result.
answerText: It managed 80 per cent of the best-case removal: 3.6 kilograms out of 4.5.

text.setup: The treatment cell has a best-case maximum. The water test tells you what it actually removed.
text.call: Check how much of the maximum it managed

estimate.prompt: The treatment could remove at most 4.5 kilograms of metal. The water test says 3.6 kilograms came out.
estimate.question: What share of the possible removal did the cell manage?
estimate.relationship: Share = what it removed ÷ what it could have removed × 100.
estimate.explanation: Divide the actual by the possible, not the other way round. Upside down gives 125 per cent, which would be a cell removing more metal than the electricity allows.
estimate.solution: 3.6 ÷ 4.5, times a hundred, is 80 per cent.

title: What the city keeps
task: Make the city-safety call before the next field report lands.
scene: The temporary laboratory is being packed up as the emergency money ends. The plant is running. The mud still holds about seventy-one kilograms. One monitoring station has funding after next month.
question: The emergency money is about to move elsewhere. What does the city keep?
takeaway: What outlasts an emergency is the part that went quiet, not the part that stopped.
why: Nothing here was destroyed. Seventy-one kilograms are in the mud, twenty were never accounted for, and something new is still being worked out. All of it is below a limit rather than gone.
answerText: Keep the monitoring, across water, mud and air. It is the only thing that would notice any of this coming back.

choices: Long-term monitoring of the water, the mud and the air.
Corrosion control, and making the plant more robust.
Open records, reference samples and written methods.
Nothing. The records can close once the review is out.
rebuttals: Corrosion control protects the pipes, and the pipes are a different hazard from the seventy-one kilograms in the mud.
Open records and reference samples preserve the method, cost very little, and should happen whatever this budget does.
Closing the records destroys the only account of how any of it was measured, and the next city starts from nothing.
text.setup: The emergency money is about to move elsewhere. What does the city keep?
